extracted.intended_audience: Practitioners before the USPTO (attorneys and patent/trademark practitioners), particularly those handling trademark matters and USPTO.gov accounts
extracted.subtask_description: Standards, procedural requirements, and sanctions governing practitioner conduct before the USPTO (with emphasis on trademark practice, USPTO.gov account sponsorship, signature rules, certifications, investigations, suspension/probation, and reinstatement).

rubrics_metrics.name: U.S. Counsel Rule (Requirement for U.S.-licensed attorney)
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective August 3, 2019, any foreign-domiciled trademark applicant or registrant must be represented before the USPTO by an attorney who is licensed to practice law in the United States. See 37 C.F.R. § 2.11(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose: (1) increase compliance with U.S. trademark law and USPTO regulations, (2) improve accuracy of trademark submissions, and (3) safeguard the integrity of the U.S. trademark register (84 Fed. Reg. 31498). Practitioners serving as U.S. counsel for foreign-domiciled clients are expected to know the U.S. Counsel Rule and its consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO trademark signature rules (personal electronic signature requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: All signatures on trademark documents must be signed by a proper person, trademark documents must be personally signed by the signatory named on the document, and a person electronically signing a document must personally enter any combination of letters, numbers, spaces, and/or punctuation marks that she or she has adopted as a signature placed between two forward slash ('/') symbols in the signature block. See 37 C.F.R. §§ 2.193(a), (c), and (e); 37 C.F.R. § 11.18(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TMEP § 611.01(c) clarifies: 'All documents must be personally signed... The person(s) identified as the signatory must manually enter the elements of the electronic signature. Another person (e.g., paralegal, legal assistant, or secretary) may not sign the name of a qualified practitioner or other authorized signatory.' Typing the electronic signature of another person is not a valid signature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences of impermissible signatures
rubrics_metrics.description: If the signature on a trademark application or other submission fails to comply with 37 C.F.R. § 2.193(a) or (e) because it was entered by someone other than the named signatory or not signed by a proper person, then the submission is improperly executed, cannot be relied upon to support registration, and normally renders the application void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case citations and agency statements: 84 Fed. Reg. at 31498; In re Yusha Zhang, 2021 TTAB LEXIS 465; In re Dermahose Inc., 82 USPQ2d 1793 (TTAB 2007); Ex parte Hipkins, 20 USPQ2d 1694 (BPAI 1991); In re Cowan, 18 USPQ2d 1407 (Comm'r Pats. 1990). Impermissible signing adversely affects integrity of federal trademark registration process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certifications when presenting papers to the USPTO (37 C.F.R. § 11.18)
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner certifies that all statements made on his or her own knowledge are true, and that all statements based on the practitioner's information and knowledge are believed to be true. The practitioner also certifies that, to the best of the party's knowledge, information and belief, formed after an inquiry reasonable under the circumstances: (i) the paper is not presented for any improper purpose; (ii) legal contentions are warranted by existing law or nonfrivolous argument; (iii) allegations and factual contentions have evidentiary support or are likely to after investigation; and (iv) denials are warranted on the evidence or reasonably based on lack of information or belief. See 37 C.F.R. § 11.18(b)(1)-(2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners presenting any paper to the USPTO thereby certify they have conducted an inquiry reasonable under the circumstances supporting factual assertions. Failing to do so risks disciplinary action under the Rules of Professional Conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable inquiry requirement supporting factual assertions
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner who presents any paper to the USPTO certifies that the practitioner has conducted an inquiry reasonable under the circumstances that supports the factual assertions set forth in the paper. See 37 C.F.R. § 11.18(b)(2)(iii).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to conduct a reasonable inquiry (e.g., not verifying specimens of use or other factual claims) can be cited as professional misconduct and grounds for discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO.gov account sponsorship rules (Verified USPTO.gov Account Agreement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Qualified attorneys are permitted to sponsor support staff who are directly employed by the attorney, the attorney's law firm, or the attorney's company, provided the support staff works under the attorney's supervision; sponsoring attorneys agree that they will not attempt to sponsor any foreign or domestic company, group, client, agent, attorney or other practitioner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sponsoring prohibited persons or entities (e.g., foreign companies or third-party vendors) violates the Agreement and may result in revocation of sponsorship privileges and disciplinary consequences. Sponsorship obligations include adequate supervision of sponsored users.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competent representation (37 C.F.R. § 11.101)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner shall provide competent representation. The Final Order finds violations where respondent failed to adequately review trademark applications, failed to establish measures to ensure sponsored support staff complied with signature rules, and violated the USPTO.gov Account Agreement by sponsoring prohibited persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Competence includes substantive knowledge of applicable laws/rules (e.g., U.S. Counsel Rule, TMEP, signature rules) and procedural safeguards to ensure filings are properly executed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable diligence in representation (37 C.F.R. § 11.103)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner must act with reasonable diligence in representing a client. Violations include failing to adequately review trademark applications, failing to ensure sponsored support staff compliance with signature rules, and improper sponsorship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diligence encompasses supervision, verification of client facts (e.g., use in commerce), and timely responses to USPTO communications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supervision of non-practitioner assistants (37 C.F.R. § 11.503(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner must adequately supervise non-practitioner assistants. The Final Order cites allowing foreign vendor employees to prepare and file applications without adequate review as a violation of § 11.503(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adequate supervision requires measures to ensure assistants comply with signature rules and that filings reflect the attorney's review and authorization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assisting in the unauthorized practice of law (37 C.F.R. § 11.505)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner must not assist in the unauthorized practice of law. Allowing foreign vendor employees to prepare and file USPTO applications without adequate oversight can constitute assisting unauthorized practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure non-U.S. persons or entities are not effectively practicing U.S. trademark law via the practitioner's sponsorship or apparent attorney-of-record status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failing to cooperate with OED or investigation (37 C.F.R. § 11.801(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner must cooperate with OED in an investigation and respond to lawful demands or requests for information from a disciplinary authority. Knowingly failing to respond to multiple lawful demands or requests is a violation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Responding to RFIs and Lack of Response Notices is mandatory; failure to respond allows OED to proceed on the information of record and is actionable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct involving misrepresentation (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: Engaging in conduct involving misrepresentation is prohibited. The Final Order cites allowing filings to bear attorney credentials so as to appear they were adequately reviewed when they were not as an example.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Misrepresentations may be found where attorney credentials mislead about the extent of attorney involvement or review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct prejudicial to the administration of the USPTO trademark registration system (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner must not engage in conduct prejudicial to the administration of the USPTO trademark registration system. Allowing improperly signed filings or sponsorship that obfuscates unauthorized practice can be prejudicial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disciplinary action may follow conduct that undermines the integrity of the registration system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practitioner address and mail-receipt obligations (37 C.F.R. § 11.11)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must provide and maintain an address for service and take reasonable steps to receive communications sent to that address (e.g., when out of the country).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to receive or act on certified mailings (RFIs, LORNs) because of lack of reasonable steps to receive mail may not excuse non-response; practitioners are reminded to ensure means to receive USPTO communications.

rubrics_metrics.name: TMEP guidance and available agency resources
rubrics_metrics.description: The Trademark Manual of Examining Procedure (TMEP) and the USPTO trademark webpages provide clear guidance on signature requirements, U.S. Counsel Rule, and other practice procedures (e.g., TMEP § 611.01(c), TMEP § 601).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners are reasonably expected to consult and know TMEP and other USPTO resources; these resources provide unambiguous information about signature requirements and ethical practice in trademark matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctions framework and suspension/reinstatement rules (37 C.F.R. §§ 11.58, 11.60, 11.56, 11.57)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office may suspend practitioners from practice and place conditions on reinstatement. The Final Order imposes a 90-day suspension, probation, and conditions for reinstatement pursuant to 37 C.F.R. § 11.58, among other provisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sanctions can include suspension, probation, loss of USPTO.gov privileges, required compliance with § 11.58, and additional suspension if probation conditions are violated. Respondent waived rights to seek reconsideration or review in this settlement, but the regulatory framework allows orders to show cause and further suspension for probation violations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrictions on USPTO.gov accounts during suspension/probation
rubrics_metrics.description: Respondent is prohibited from opening, activating, applying for, verifying, or sponsoring any USPTO.gov account(s) for preparing or filing documents with the USPTO until reinstated; USPTO is authorized to disable or suspend all USPTO.gov accounts registered to Respondent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Immediate prohibition on using or assisting others in using any USPTO.gov accounts upon expiration of limited recognition; Respondent cannot have her name added to others' verified accounts until reinstated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Client notification procedures for foreign-domiciled clients during suspension (37 C.F.R. § 11.58(c)(3)(i))
rubrics_metrics.description: Respondent may satisfy obligations for foreign-domiciled clients by emailing in the client's native language the requisite 37 C.F.R. § 11.58 notices and information (including a correctly translated Final Order) to: (1) the client's email address (if reasonably believed to be directly accessible by client), (2) an email address belonging to the client with direct access, or (3) the foreign-domiciled third person or referring entity only if certain reasonable measures are taken (forwarding, confirmation of receipt, and affidavit detailing measures).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If using a referring entity to forward notices, respondent must: A) ensure it promptly forwards with respondent copied, B) take measures to learn the client actually received the email and translated Final Order, and C) set forth details of reasonable measures in the § 11.58(d) affidavit and any petition for reinstatement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited recognition period to conclude client matters (37 C.F.R. § 11.58(f))
rubrics_metrics.description: Respondent is granted limited recognition for thirty (30) days from the Final Order date so she may conclude work on clients' matters pending before the Office; if work cannot be concluded within 30 days, respondent must advise each client.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After the 30-day limited recognition period expires, respondent is prohibited from using USPTO.gov accounts and must not assist others to use them for filing with the USPTO.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation to identify and declare improperly signed filings
rubrics_metrics.description: Within twenty-one (21) days of the Final Order, respondent shall send a letter listing all applications and trademark documents on which respondent is the named signatory but did not sign the application or document, including type of document, filing date, and application serial/registration number, and accompanied by a declaration/affidavit in compliance with 28 U.S.C. § 1746 stating she did not sign the document.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The list should include the 441 identified applications and any others where the named signatory did not sign; the declaration must be compliant with 28 U.S.C. § 1746.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cooperation with USPTO inquiries into improper filings
rubrics_metrics.description: Respondent shall cooperate fully with the USPTO in any present or future USPTO inquiry made into improper filings by the foreign vendor or any persons/entities with whom respondent worked in connection with trademark documents submitted to the USPTO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Full cooperation includes responding to RFIs, providing records and evidence, and complying with OED requests as part of settlement terms and ongoing obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probation monitoring requirements (searches and reporting)
rubrics_metrics.description: During probation, respondent must: (i) at least monthly, search TESS (or replacement) for applications identifying her as attorney of record and promptly inform in writing the USPTO Office of Trademark Examination Policy of filings identifying her as attorney of record that were made without her knowledge or consent; and (ii) at least quarterly, submit a written report to the OED Director certifying completion of monthly searches and either stating no improper filings were found or providing copies of correspondence sent to the Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reports must document the monthly searches and any corrective communications made to USPTO Office of Trademark Examination Policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuing legal education and TMEP review as reinstatement conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: As a condition of being reinstated to practice before the USPTO, respondent must provide an affidavit declaring she has successfully completed 12 hours of CLE credit on ethics/professional responsibility and has reviewed thoroughly all provisions of the TMEP, including signature requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Declarations must comply with 28 U.S.C. § 1746 and be submitted to the OED Director with details of completion.

rubrics_metrics.name: OED authority to seek discrete discipline and additional sanctions
rubrics_metrics.description: OED Director may issue an Order to Show Cause and request the USPTO Director impose additional suspension (up to nine months) if respondent, during probation, fails to comply with any provision of the Agreement, Final Order, or Rules of Professional Conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural steps include sending the Order to Show Cause, granting 15 days to respond, and forwarding to USPTO Director to request immediate suspension; discrete discipline for misconduct underlying the Order to Show Cause may also be sought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication and public notice of disciplinary action
rubrics_metrics.description: The OED Director shall electronically publish the Final Order publicly (including the OED electronic FOIA Reading Room) and publish a notice materially consistent with the provided Notice of Suspension and Probation in the Official Gazette.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publication serves to notify the public and practitioners of disciplinary findings, procedures violated, and consequences; the Notice summarizes the conduct, violated rules, and advice to practitioners (e.g., maintaining means to receive USPTO communications).

rubrics_metrics.name: Financial responsibility for USPTO costs (37 C.F.R. § 11.60)
rubrics_metrics.description: As a condition of probation and reinstatement, respondent shall pay in full the USPTO's allowable costs described in 37 C.F.R. § 11.60 incurred in connection with the institution, prosecution, and dismissal of the formal disciplinary proceeding within sixty (60) days of being informed in writing of such costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to pay may affect reinstatement and further disciplinary status.
